title: Weighted Vendi score
purpose: Measure the effective number of distinct members in a weighted set from a similarity matrix or feature rows. Use it to compare the diversity of samples, prompts, solutions or ensemble members when members carry unequal weight or appear as duplicates.

entry_points.name: weighted_vendi_score
entry_points.arguments: similarity: n by n symmetric positive semidefinite matrix with unit diagonal; weights: n non-negative numbers with a positive sum, or null for equal weights; order: Renyi order q >= 0 (default 1)
entry_points.returns: {score, order, eigenvalues: normalized and descending, weights: normalized, members}

entry_points.name: vendi_from_features
entry_points.arguments: features: n non-zero rows of equal length; weights; order
entry_points.returns: the weighted_vendi_score result plus similarity, the cosine matrix scored

assumptions: The similarity matrix is a valid kernel: symmetric, positive semidefinite, with k(x, x) = 1.
Weights express how much each row counts; rows with weight 0 do not affect the score.
guarantees: n mutually orthogonal members with equal weights score n; identical members score 1.
Splitting a member into identical clones whose weights sum to its weight leaves the score unchanged.
The score lies between 1 and the number of members with positive weight and does not increase with the order q.
Inputs that are not symmetric, not positive semidefinite or not unit-diagonal raise ValueError.

known_wrong.name: clones_not_counted_as_members
known_wrong.why: An unweighted score counts each clone as a separate member; with conserved weights the two clones are one member.

limits: Dense eigendecomposition by Jacobi rotations: intended for at most a few hundred members. Eigenvalues at or below 1e-12 are treated as zero, which matters for orders below 1. The score depends entirely on the chosen kernel; it says nothing about quality, coverage of a target distribution or usefulness of the members.
technique_references: Vendi Score: a diversity evaluation metric for machine learning (Friedman and Dieng)
